headline: The Public Secret That Hedge Funds Use to Beat Markets
lede: The Freedom of Information Act was written for journalists and aggrieved citizens. A small class of hedge funds quietly discovered it was also a perfectly legal back door into the regulatory state — and built trading edges that retail investors can file for but rarely, in practice, exploit.
body:
The mechanics are straightforward enough to explain in a sentence: a hedge fund submits a FOIA request to the Food and Drug Administration asking for inspection records, warning letters, or *Form 483* reports (the FDA’s shorthand for written observations made by inspectors during facility visits) about a specific drug manufacturer or contract research organisation. The government, bound by statute, eventually responds. The fund reads the documents, decides whether the news is good or bad, and trades accordingly. Because the information was obtained through a public-records request — technically available to anyone with a stamp and a cover letter — it falls outside the legal definition of *material non-public information*, the category of tips that securities law forbids. The strategy is, in the language of compliance officers, clean.

The canonical illustration comes from the fourth quarter of 2011, when SAC Capital Advisors — the Stamford, Connecticut fund founded by Steven Cohen, later the subject of a guilty plea by his firm for securities fraud on separate insider-trading charges — filed a FOIA request with the FDA seeking inspection records for Charles River Laboratories (CRL), a company that provides contract research services to the pharmaceutical industry. Whatever the documents conveyed, it apparently gave SAC comfort: the fund increased its position in CRL from roughly 70,000 shares to about 240,000 in the same quarter it made the request. The stock subsequently rose, and SAC sold most of the position in the following quarter, netting a gain the University of Maryland researchers who documented the episode estimated at between 26 and 32 percent. No law was broken. The information was public. The edge was in knowing to ask.

The academic study that surfaced this pattern — "The Freedom of Information Act and the Race Towards Information Acquisition," by Antonio Gargano, Alberto G. Rossi, and Russ Wermers, published in *The Review of Financial Studies* in 2017 — examined 529 cases between 1995 and 2013 where institutional investors filed FOIA requests directly about specific publicly traded companies. The findings were striking: stocks bought in the same quarter a FOIA request was filed posted abnormal gains of 5.26 percent; stocks sold following a FOIA filing dropped an abnormal 3.09 percent. These are not rounding errors. They imply that the investors filing these requests were, on average, receiving meaningful signal — and acting on it profitably before the information diffused into market prices through other channels. More recent episodes extend the pattern: Deep Track Capital, a $5.2 billion Greenwich fund focused on life sciences, filed a December 2024 FOIA request for FDA Form 483 inspection reports on CG Oncology, a biotech developing oncolytic immunotherapies. Within days, CG Oncology announced positive Phase 3 trial results and the stock jumped 30 percent on a single day in January 2025. Point72, Exodus Point, and J.P. Morgan were among other financial institutions filing FDA requests around the same time.

The central legal question — why is this not insider trading? — hinges on where "public" ends and "non-public" begins. Securities law prohibits trading on *material non-public information*, and the word "non-public" has been interpreted by courts to mean information not generally available to investors. FOIA responses, once delivered, are technically public records. The argument is that a document sitting in a government filing system, obtainable by anyone who submits the correct form and waits, is not secret merely because almost nobody has bothered to ask for it. The SEC has not moved to challenge this interpretation. The gap between "available to the public" and "actually known to the public" is where the alpha lives — and where the strategy’s critics argue the spirit of the law diverges from its letter.

The structural reason most investors cannot replicate this edge is not legal but logistical. The FDA processes FOIA requests on timelines measured in months, not days; a 2024 analysis found that only about 80 percent of FDA FOIA requests were resolved within 200 days of submission, roughly eight months, with roughly 12 percent remaining open beyond 400 days. A sophisticated fund manages this latency by filing requests speculatively, well in advance of any trade thesis, building what amounts to a proprietary regulatory-intelligence pipeline. It employs dedicated legal staff who know which exemptions the FDA typically applies, how to frame requests for maximum yield, and how to parse the resulting documents — inspection jargon, *corrective action* timescales, repeat observation patterns — in ways that translate into an investment view. The information, in other words, is public in the same sense that the Library of Congress is public: in principle accessible to anyone, in practice navigable only by those with the time, training, and resources to work it systematically. For a retail investor with a brokerage account and a day job, filing a FOIA request about a pharmaceutical contractor is possible. Building a trading strategy around the output is another matter entirely.

concepts.definition: A 1966 US federal law requiring government agencies to disclose records upon request, subject to enumerated exemptions. Any person or entity can submit a FOIA request to agencies such as the FDA, FAA, or Department of Labor; the agency must respond, though it may withhold documents under exemptions covering trade secrets, ongoing investigations, or personal privacy. The law was designed to make government accountable to citizens and journalists; its use by financial institutions as a source of investment intelligence was an unintended but legally sanctioned application.

Any dataset used by investors that falls outside conventional financial disclosures — earnings releases, SEC filings, analyst estimates. The category spans satellite imagery of retail parking lots, credit-card transaction flows, shipping-container manifests, job-posting counts, and, increasingly, systematically harvested government regulatory records obtained via FOIA. The alternative-data industry was estimated to be worth several billion dollars annually by the mid-2020s; FOIA-sourced regulatory intelligence represents a niche but legally uncomplicated corner of it.

An FDA document issued at the close of a facility inspection listing observations — deviations from good manufacturing practice that inspectors noted but that have not yet risen to the level of a formal warning letter. A Form 483 with many observations, or repeat observations from prior inspections, can signal manufacturing quality problems before they are publicly disclosed in enforcement actions, making them valuable inputs for investors in pharmaceutical and biotech companies.

The legal concept at the heart of insider-trading law. Information is material if a reasonable investor would consider it significant in deciding whether to buy or sell a security; it is non-public if it has not been disseminated in a way that makes it genuinely available to the investing public. FOIA-obtained information occupies a contested gray zone: technically public because it was obtained through a lawful public-records process, yet not broadly known. The SEC has not issued definitive guidance ruling FOIA-based trading strategies illegal.

fact_check: The core facts check out. The SAC Capital / Charles River Laboratories trade in Q4 2011 — a position increase from roughly 70,000 to 240,000 shares following a FOIA request to the FDA, with subsequent gains of 26-32 percent — is documented in the Gargano, Rossi, and Wermers paper published in The Review of Financial Studies (2017) and reported by The Wall Street Journal (2013). The 5.26 percent abnormal return on buy trades and 3.09 percent abnormal return on sell trades are from the same peer-reviewed study. The Deep Track Capital / CG Oncology episode is contemporaneously documented in coverage from early 2025. One note of caution: the tweet’s framing implies FOIA was the decisive factor in SAC’s CRL trade; the academic literature treats this as a representative example, not a proven causal chain. SAC was also under an intense, multi-year insider-trading investigation during this period for unrelated positions, which does not taint the CRL trade legally but is context worth keeping in mind.
